The clock on the tower at Orlen Cross stopped at ten past four one Tuesday in March. My grandfather, Aurel Moss, had kept it for forty-one years, climbing the worn iron ladder each Sunday to wind it, and that spring I had begun to climb with him. He had done the Sunday winding two days before, and on Monday the Harl bus had left by the clock to the minute.

We went up together after breakfast. Pigeons had built their nests on the outer ledge, birds settling in for the spring, and a skin of ice still clung to the face, but the hands moved freely when he tried them. Every pin in the escapement was sound; he had renewed each worn part the spring before. Then he shone his torch down the shaft beside the gears. The weight cable had slipped off its drum and lay in coils on the floor below.

At the council meeting that evening, Jonas Brede from the hardware shop brought a catalogue of new electric works to replace the old. Petra Vell, who chaired the council, had borrowed my grandfather's notebook, and she read from it aloud: every repair since 1983, each with its cost, totalled at the foot of the page in her red ink. Someone mentioned the spring fair, three weeks off, and someone else my grandfather's safety on the ladder. Petra read out the total again, and the vote went six to one to replace the old works with Jonas's cheapest model.

Before the meeting closed, Petra struck the keeper's wage from the town accounts, eleven pounds a month that he had drawn since before I was born. Nobody asked him about it. Jonas fitted his grey box beside the old gears the next week and handed my grandfather the old pendulum.

The clock keeps good time now, and the bell rings on the hour. Petra Vell turned forty-one years of his Sundays into a column of figures and then voted him out of a job in the same hour, while the council sat and let her. It was wrong, and at the fair I told her so to her face.

passage:
Lune's starwort, a pale blue flower about the size of a thumbnail, grows only on the north slope of Corrow Ridge. For a decade its seed heads have come up nearly empty, a serious matter for a plant that lives only four or five years. In 2023 the park's warden, Petra Moss, asked Ines Varga, an ecologist at Pellham University, to find out why.

Everyone at Corrow had an explanation. Moss blamed the dry summers. Aldo Brisk, who has grazed his sheep on the slope for more than thirty years, blamed the late frosts. Varga decided to test every idea at once. Her student, Tobin Hale, staked out twenty-five plots where the starwort still grew thickest. Some were fenced against the sheep, some sheltered under cloths on frosty nights, some watered in dry weeks to keep the soil moist through the summer, and some cleared of crowding grass. On the last set Hale did the bees' work himself with a paintbrush, dabbing pollen from flower to flower.

In September Ruth Callan, who teaches at the village school in Ottery, brought her pupils up to count seeds. One set of plots stood out: the fenced plots held about forty seeds a head, against four or five everywhere else on the slope. The sheep, it turned out, had been nipping off the flower heads before the seed could ripen.

The board met in October, beneath the 1988 photograph that hangs in its meeting room, in which sheep graze among the flowers. Its members pointed to the photograph, set aside a summer of counted seed, and voted to keep Brisk's flock on the slope. They adopted Moss's explanation instead: from June her wardens will truck water up the ridge twice a week.

The Ottery Courier, which sent a reporter to cover the vote, called the result a sensible compromise. It was nothing of the kind. A photograph records one afternoon in 1988; Callan's pupils counted every seed head on the slope. The watered plots ended the summer as empty as the rest. The board was shown what is harming the starwort, and it has chosen to spend its money on something else.
